title: Alcohol and GABA: How Drinking Affects Your Brain's Calm
excerpt: How alcohol boosts GABA and blocks glutamate, why the rebound causes 3am wake-ups and hangxiety, which GABA medicines don't mix with drinking, and whether GABA supplements help.
metaDescription: How alcohol affects GABA, why the rebound causes 3am wake-ups and hangxiety, which calming drugs don't mix with alcohol, and if GABA supplements help.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The short answer:** alcohol works largely by boosting GABA, your brain's main calming chemical messenger, while turning down glutamate, its main excitatory one. That combination is why a drink or two feels relaxing. It's also why the next morning can feel jittery, anxious, or wide awake at 3am: as alcohol leaves your body, the calming boost vanishes faster than your brain's counter-adjustments do. This guide explains that seesaw in plain words, what it means for sleep and next-day anxiety, why it makes alcohol risky with certain medicines, and whether GABA supplements are worth a look.

**The quick rules:** don't mix alcohol with sedating medicines (benzodiazepines, sleeping pills, gabapentin, pregabalin, strong antihistamines, opioids) without a doctor's okay. Don't treat a hangover with "calming" pills or another drink. If you want to try a GABA supplement, keep it off drinking nights. And give your last drink a few hours before bed so the rebound happens while you're awake, not at 3am.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research about how alcohol affects the brain. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor** before drinking if you take any medicine that causes drowsiness, and before starting a supplement if you take prescription medication. **Get medical help right away** if you or someone else has shaking, sweating, a racing heart, confusion, or seeing or hearing things that aren't there after cutting back from heavy daily drinking, or has a seizure. Call 911 for slow or irregular breathing, someone who can't be woken, or a seizure.

## What GABA Is, in Plain Words

Your brain runs on a balance between signals that say "go" and signals that say "slow down." The main "go" messenger is **glutamate**. The main "slow down" messenger is **GABA**, short for gamma-aminobutyric acid. GABA is made inside the brain and released by nerve cells to quiet down their neighbors.

GABA does its job by attaching to receptors, which work like locks on the surface of nerve cells. There are two main families:

- **GABA-A receptors** are fast-acting channels. When GABA binds, the channel opens and lets negatively charged chloride into the cell, making it harder for that nerve cell to fire. This is the system that benzodiazepines (Xanax, Valium, Ativan), barbiturates, many sleep drugs, and some anesthetics act on.
- **GABA-B receptors** act more slowly through chemical messages inside the cell. Baclofen, a muscle relaxant, and phenibut, a drug sold online as a supplement, work here.

When the "slow down" side is well balanced against the "go" side, you feel alert but calm. Tip it too far toward GABA and you get drowsy, clumsy, and slow. Tip it too far toward glutamate and you get anxious, restless, and in extreme cases, prone to seizures.

## How Alcohol Affects GABA

Alcohol (ethanol) is a small, simple molecule that touches a lot of brain systems, but its effect on GABA is among the best studied and most important.

### It makes GABA-A receptors respond more strongly

Alcohol doesn't sit in the same spot GABA does. Instead, it acts as what pharmacologists call a **positive modulator**: it changes the shape of the GABA-A receptor so that the GABA already present has a bigger effect. More chloride flows in, nerve cells are quieter, and the brain's "slow down" signal gets louder. Researchers have found that certain types of GABA-A receptors, including ones found outside the main nerve connections that set the brain's background level of calm, may be especially sensitive to alcohol, though scientists still debate the details.

Animal studies also show that alcohol can increase the release of GABA in some brain regions, so it may turn up both the volume of the signal and the sensitivity of the receivers.

### It turns down glutamate at the same time

Alcohol also blocks NMDA receptors, one of the main types of glutamate receptor. That weakens the brain's "go" signal. NMDA receptors are central to forming new memories, which is one reason heavy drinking can lead to patchy memory or blackouts.

So alcohol pushes on both sides of the seesaw at once: more braking, less accelerating. That's a powerful combination, and it explains the familiar arc of a night of drinking.

### What that feels like at different levels

- **One or two drinks:** a mild calming effect, lower social anxiety, a bit more talkative. The GABA boost is gentle and the frontal brain areas that handle self-restraint are among the first to quiet down.
- **Several drinks:** slower reactions, poorer coordination, slurred speech, and worse judgment as the effect spreads to the cerebellum (movement) and other areas.
- **Heavy drinking:** strong sedation, memory gaps, and at very high levels, suppression of the brain areas that control breathing and gag reflexes. That's what makes alcohol poisoning dangerous.

GABA is not the only system involved. Alcohol also releases dopamine and the body's own opioid-like chemicals (endorphins), which contribute to the pleasant "buzz," and it affects serotonin and adenosine, a sleep-pressure chemical. But the GABA and glutamate seesaw is the backbone of alcohol's calming, sedating effects.

## The Rebound: Why the Next Morning Feels Wired

Here's the part that matters most for social drinkers. Your brain constantly adjusts to keep itself in balance. When alcohol is pushing the "slow down" side, the brain starts pushing back toward "go," dialing down the GABA response a little and turning up excitatory activity.

While alcohol is still in your blood, those adjustments are hidden. Once your liver clears the alcohol, which happens at roughly one standard drink per hour for many people, the extra GABA boost disappears. The counter-adjustments, though, take longer to unwind. For a while, the seesaw tips the other way: less braking, more accelerating.

Researchers often describe this as a mini version of withdrawal. After a single night of moderate drinking it's mild and short-lived, but it lines up with a lot of common next-day complaints:

- Feeling restless, edgy, or on alert
- Next-day anxiety or a sense of dread, often called "hangxiety"
- Sensitivity to light and noise
- Light, broken sleep in the second half of the night
- A faster heartbeat or feeling shaky

To be honest about the evidence: the GABA rebound is a leading explanation for these symptoms, not a fully proven one. Human studies of hangovers are hard to run, and dehydration, low blood sugar, inflammation, poor sleep, and stress hormones all play their part. But the rebound idea fits well with what we know from animal research and from the more severe version seen in heavy drinkers.

## Alcohol, GABA, and the 3am Wake-Up

Many people notice they fall asleep fast after drinking, then wake up in the early hours, alert and unable to drop back off. The GABA story explains a lot of this. (For the drowsy first half of the night on its own, see [why alcohol makes you sleepy](/never-hungover/why-does-alcohol-make-you-sleepy).)

Early in the night, while your blood alcohol is high, the extra GABA push makes falling asleep easier and deepens the first stretch of sleep. Alcohol also tends to suppress REM sleep, the dreaming stage, during that first half. By the middle of the night, your liver has cleared much of the alcohol. The calming effect fades, the brain's excitatory counter-adjustments are still running, and sleep turns light and fragmented. REM can come back with a rush, sometimes with vivid dreams. Add a full bladder, a faster heartbeat, and dehydration, and 3am wake-ups become very common.

What helps:

- **Stop drinking two to three hours before bed** so more of the alcohol is cleared, and more of the rebound happens, while you're still awake.
- **Drink less in total.** The rebound scales with how much you drank.
- **Alternate with water** and eat a proper meal, which slows absorption.
- **Don't reach for a "calming" pill** to fall back asleep if there's still alcohol in your system.

For more on the sleep side, see our guide to [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) and our deeper look at [alcohol and REM sleep](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-rem-sleep-complete-scientific-analysis-2025).

## GABA and Hangxiety

"Hangxiety" is the anxious, guilty, on-edge feeling some people get the day after drinking. If you've ever felt a wave of dread on a Sunday morning even though nothing bad happened on Saturday night, the GABA and glutamate seesaw is a big part of the reason. Your brain spent the evening with its brakes artificially boosted, and now it's briefly running with them weakened.

Not everyone gets it equally. Research from University College London and the University of Exeter, published in 2019, found that very shy people tended to report more next-day anxiety after drinking than less shy people. That fits with the idea that people who use alcohol to take the edge off social nerves feel the rebound more.

Practical ways to soften it:

- Keep to a pace your body can clear, roughly one drink an hour at most, with water in between.
- Protect your sleep, since short, broken sleep makes anxiety worse on its own.
- Eat something with protein and complex carbohydrates the next morning.
- Get outside and move a little. Light exercise helps many people feel steadier.
- Remember the feeling is partly chemical and usually passes within a day.

Our [complete guide to hangxiety](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research) covers the research and practical fixes in more detail. If anxiety after drinking is regular, intense, or starting to shape how you feel day to day, that's worth raising with a doctor. It's common and very treatable.

## Tolerance: How Regular Drinking Rewires the GABA System

If you drink often, your brain doesn't just make short-term adjustments. It makes longer-lasting ones. Over weeks and months of regular heavy drinking, research shows the brain changes which building blocks its GABA-A receptors are made from and how many of them sit on the surface of nerve cells, making them less responsive to both GABA and alcohol. At the same time, glutamate NMDA receptors become more numerous or more sensitive.

That's the biological basis of **tolerance**: you need more alcohol to feel the same effect, because the brain has turned down the very system alcohol acts on. It's also why regular heavy drinkers often feel anxious, irritable, and sleep poorly even when they're not drinking. The baseline balance has shifted toward "go." For a fuller explanation, see our guide to [alcohol tolerance](/never-hungover/alcohol-tolerance).

### Why stopping suddenly after heavy daily drinking can be dangerous

When someone who has been drinking heavily every day for weeks or longer suddenly stops, the boosted alcohol signal vanishes, and the brain is left with weakened brakes and an overactive accelerator. That's **alcohol withdrawal**, and unlike a hangover it can be a medical emergency. Symptoms can include shaking, sweating, a racing heart, high blood pressure, anxiety, insomnia, nausea, and in severe cases seizures, hallucinations, and a dangerous state of confusion called delirium tremens.

Doctors usually treat alcohol withdrawal with benzodiazepines, which act on the same GABA-A receptors. They are essentially standing in for alcohol in a controlled way and then being tapered down. That treatment only makes sense under medical supervision.

This is not something a typical weekend social drinker needs to worry about after one big night. But if you've been drinking a lot every day and want to cut back, talk to a doctor first rather than stopping cold turkey.

> **When to see a doctor.** A rough morning after a night out is normal. These are not:
> - Shaking, sweating, a racing heart, or confusion that starts **6 to 48 hours after cutting back** from heavy daily drinking
> - Seeing, hearing, or feeling things that aren't there
> - A seizure, or fainting
> - Anxiety or insomnia that persists for days after drinking, or that is getting worse over time
> - Needing a drink in the morning to stop feeling shaky
>
> For a seizure, slow or irregular breathing, or someone who can't be woken, **call 911**. For the others, contact a doctor or urgent care the same day. If you're worried about how much you're drinking, your doctor can help without judgment, and in the US the free, confidential SAMHSA National Helpline is available at 1-800-662-4357.

## Why GABA Matters for Medication Safety

Because alcohol leans heavily on the GABA system, it adds to the effects of anything else that calms the brain. Combining two or more of these is where most serious alcohol and medication accidents come from. The effects don't just add up; they can multiply, especially for breathing.

The most important combinations to avoid or discuss with your doctor:

- **Benzodiazepines** such as alprazolam (Xanax), diazepam (Valium), lorazepam (Ativan), and clonazepam (Klonopin). These act directly on GABA-A receptors, the same target as alcohol. Together they can cause deep sedation, blackouts, falls, and slowed breathing. See our guide to [Xanax and alcohol](/never-hungover/xanax-and-alcohol).
- **Sleep medicines** such as zolpidem (Ambien) and eszopiclone (Lunesta), which also act on GABA-A receptors. Combining them with alcohol raises the risk of sleepwalking, sleep-driving, and other complex sleep behaviors, plus breathing problems.
- **Gabapentin and pregabalin (Lyrica).** These don't work directly on GABA receptors despite the name, but they calm nerve activity in other ways. In 2019 the FDA warned about serious breathing problems when these drugs are combined with other central nervous system depressants. See our guide to [gabapentin and alcohol](/never-hungover/gabapentin-and-alcohol).
- **Opioid pain medicines.** The FDA added boxed warnings to opioids and benzodiazepines in 2016 about the danger of combining them, and alcohol carries similar risks.
- **Muscle relaxers, sedating antihistamines (like diphenhydramine), and some antidepressants and antipsychotics** can all add drowsiness.
- **Phenibut**, sometimes sold online as a supplement for anxiety or sleep, acts on GABA-B receptors. It carries real risks of dependence and severe withdrawal on its own, and combining it with alcohol can cause dangerous sedation. Poison control centers have reported a rise in phenibut exposures in recent years. Skip it.

If you take any of these, the safest step is to ask your doctor or pharmacist directly whether you can drink at all, and if so, how much. Don't take an extra dose of a sedating medicine to "sleep off" a night of drinking.

## GABA Supplements and Alcohol: Do They Help, and Are They Safe?

Plain GABA is sold as a supplement for stress and sleep, and it's natural to wonder whether it could replace some of what alcohol does, or fix the rebound the next day. Here's where the evidence stands.

### Does oral GABA reach the brain?

This is the big open question. For decades the standard view was that GABA taken by mouth doesn't cross the blood-brain barrier, the protective filter between the bloodstream and the brain, in meaningful amounts. More recent reviews say the evidence is mixed: some small human studies report modest effects on stress markers or sleep, but it isn't clear whether those effects come from GABA reaching the brain, from signals through the gut and nerves, or from chance. Studies tend to be small, short, and sometimes funded by manufacturers. In short, oral GABA's effects, if any, appear to be mild.

### Is it safe to take GABA with alcohol?

There's very little direct research on combining oral GABA supplements with alcohol, so nobody can promise it's safe. Given how weak oral GABA appears to be, the combination is unlikely to be dramatic for most people, but any calming product taken on top of alcohol adds some sedation, and supplements aren't held to the same testing standards as drugs. The sensible approach:

- **Don't take GABA (or other calming supplements) on drinking nights.**
- **Don't use it alongside prescription sedatives** without asking your doctor or pharmacist.
- **Choose products that have been third-party tested,** and stick to the label dose.
- **Never confuse GABA with phenibut.** They're very different in strength and risk.

### What about using GABA for a hangover?

There's no good evidence that GABA supplements relieve hangovers or hangxiety. Sleep, hydration, food, time, and drinking less the night before remain the approaches with the most support. We go deeper into the research on GABA itself in our [complete guide to GABA supplements](/never-hungover/gaba-gamma-aminobutyric-acid-complete-guide-benefits-dosage-natural-sources-2025).

### Other "GABA-ish" supplements people ask about

- **L-theanine,** found in tea, may promote a calm, alert state (see our guide to [L-theanine and alcohol](/never-hungover/l-theanine-and-alcohol)). It's generally well tolerated, but evidence for hangover relief is thin.
- **Magnesium** helps regulate nerve signaling, and heavy drinking can lower magnesium levels. It's reasonable to eat magnesium-rich foods; supplements are best discussed with a doctor if you have kidney problems.
- **Kava** acts partly on GABA-A receptors. Combining kava with alcohol raises sedation and has been linked to concerns about liver injury, so it's best not to mix them. See our guide to [kava and alcohol](/never-hungover/kava-and-alcohol).
- **Valerian** is used as a sleep aid and may add drowsiness with alcohol.

## DHM and the GABA Connection

Dihydromyricetin (DHM), a compound from the Japanese raisin tree, first drew scientific attention for exactly this reason. A 2012 study by Shen and colleagues at UCLA, published in the *Journal of Neuroscience*, found that in rats, DHM counteracted some of alcohol's effects on GABA-A receptors. Rats given DHM showed fewer signs of intoxication, and the researchers also saw reduced signs of withdrawal and lower voluntary drinking. Other lab and animal work has explored DHM's effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver.

It's important to be clear about the limits. Those findings come mainly from rats and lab studies. Human research is small, and there is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers, blocks the GABA rebound, or protects the brain from alcohol in people. It also does not make it safe to drink while taking benzodiazepines, sleeping pills, or other sedatives. Our explainer on [the science behind DHM](/never-hungover/dhm-science-explained) goes through what the studies did and didn't show.

If you're curious to try it as part of a sensible drinking plan, popular choices include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people typically take and when. If you take any prescription medication, check with your pharmacist first; our [DHM medication interactions guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) is a good starting point. None of this replaces the basics: pacing, water, food, and sleep.

## Practical Takeaways for Social Drinkers

Understanding the GABA seesaw turns a lot of familiar hangover advice into common sense:

1. **Pace yourself.** The faster and higher your blood alcohol rises, the bigger the swing on the way down.
2. **Finish early.** A last drink two to three hours before bed lets more of the rebound pass while you're awake.
3. **Don't stack depressants.** Alcohol plus sleeping pills, benzodiazepines, gabapentin, opioids, or phenibut is where real danger lies.
4. **Don't "fix" the morning with more alcohol.** A morning drink just delays the rebound and is a warning sign if it becomes a habit.
5. **Expect next-day anxiety to pass.** It's partly chemistry. Food, water, daylight, and a gentle walk help.
6. **Notice patterns.** Needing more to feel the same, sleeping badly on non-drinking nights, or feeling shaky after cutting back are signs your GABA system has adapted. That's worth a chat with a doctor.

For a broader plan, our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through the habits with the best evidence.

## The Bottom Line

Alcohol's calm comes largely from borrowing your brain's GABA system: it makes GABA-A receptors respond more strongly and quiets glutamate. When the alcohol wears off, that borrowed calm is paid back as restlessness, broken sleep, and sometimes anxiety. For an occasional social drinker, that rebound is short-lived and manageable with pacing, food, water, and sleep. For regular heavy drinkers, the same system adapts in ways that can make stopping suddenly dangerous. Because alcohol relies on GABA, it's risky to mix with other calming drugs, and there's no good evidence that GABA supplements fix a hangover.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How does alcohol affect GABA?**

Alcohol makes GABA-A receptors, the brain's main calming switches, respond more strongly than usual, so the 'slow down' signal gets louder. At the same time it dampens glutamate, the main 'speed up' signal, at NMDA receptors. Together those two effects explain the relaxation, loosened inhibitions, slower reactions, and sleepiness of drinking. As alcohol leaves your body, the extra GABA boost disappears while the brain's short-term adjustments linger, which is one reason people can feel restless, anxious, or wide awake the next morning.

**Does alcohol increase GABA levels in the brain?**

Not mainly by making more GABA. Alcohol's best-studied effect is on the GABA-A receptor itself: it makes the receptor respond more to the GABA that is already there. Animal research also shows alcohol can increase GABA release in some brain areas. The practical result is the same either way: more calming signal while you drink, followed by a rebound as alcohol wears off.

**Can I take a GABA supplement with alcohol?**

There is very little research on combining oral GABA supplements with alcohol, so nobody can tell you it is safe with confidence. Oral GABA appears to have mild effects at most, partly because it's unclear how much reaches the brain, but stacking any calming product on top of alcohol adds sedation. If you want to try GABA, don't take it on drinking nights, and ask a doctor or pharmacist first if you take any sedating medicine. Avoid phenibut entirely with alcohol; it's a much stronger GABA-B drug with serious dependence and overdose risks.

**Why do I wake up at 3am after drinking?**

Alcohol helps you fall asleep partly through its GABA effect. As your liver clears it in the middle of the night, that calming push fades while the brain's opposing 'excitatory' adjustments are still running, and sleep becomes lighter and more broken. Needing to urinate, a faster heart rate, and low blood sugar can add to it. Stopping drinks a few hours before bed and drinking less overall are the most reliable fixes.

**Is hangxiety caused by GABA?**

GABA rebound is one of the leading explanations for next-day anxiety, but it is not the whole story. Poor sleep, dehydration, low blood sugar, stress hormones, and embarrassment about the night before all play a part, and research on hangxiety in humans is still limited. The GABA and glutamate seesaw explains why the feeling can show up even when nothing bad happened.

**Is it dangerous to mix alcohol with benzodiazepines, gabapentin, or sleeping pills?**

Yes. Benzodiazepines like Xanax and Valium, sleep drugs like Ambien, and gabapentin or pregabalin all calm the nervous system, and several act on the same GABA system alcohol does. Combined with alcohol they can cause heavy sedation, blackouts, falls, and dangerously slowed breathing. The FDA has issued warnings about breathing problems when these drugs are combined with other central nervous system depressants. Talk to your doctor before drinking on any of them.

**Does DHM work on GABA receptors?**

In animal research, yes. A 2012 study in rats published in the Journal of Neuroscience found that DHM blocked some of alcohol's effects on GABA-A receptors and reduced signs of intoxication and withdrawal. That has not been confirmed in good human trials, and there is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers or protects the brain from alcohol in people. It's an interesting lead, not a proven fix.

**How long does it take for GABA to return to normal after drinking?**

After a single night of social drinking, most people feel back to normal within a day, once sleep catches up. After long periods of heavy daily drinking, the brain's GABA and glutamate systems take much longer to rebalance, and stopping suddenly can trigger withdrawal that needs medical care. If you drink heavily every day, don't quit cold turkey without talking to a doctor.
